articles.title: The Federal Circuit Expands Its Jurisdiction Yet Again
articles.content:
Professor Paul Gugliuzza (UTexas) argues in this guest post that the Federal Circuit got the jurisdictional question in Insulet v. EOFlow wrong. He has filed an amicus brief supporting Insulet’s pending petition for rehearing en banc, and makes his case below. — Dennis
Guest post by Professor Paul R. Gugliuzza
Since Congress created the Federal Circuit in 1982, the court has repeatedly expanded the class of cases that, in its view, “arise under” patent law and so fall within its exclusive jurisdiction. The court’s recent decision in Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow Co. is another example. Insulet is a trade secret case. Yet the Federal Circuit held that the case arose under patent law based on its prediction about the outcome of a hypothetical future patent infringement dispute.
The court’s decision overlooks a fundamental principle of the law of federal jurisdiction: namely, that the “arising under” analysis looks solely at the plaintiff’s well-pleaded complaint, not to issues that may (or may not) arise in future litigation.
Some background. In Insulet, the district court entered a $60 million judgment for Insulet on a jury verdict of trade secret misappropriation. Insulet’s original complaint had asserted patent claims, too, but those claims were bifurcated from the trade secret claims, never adjudicated, and eventually dismissed without prejudice by an amendment to Insulet’s complaint.
EOFlow appealed its trial loss to the Federal Circuit. Insulet contested jurisdiction because its amended complaint contained no patent claims, citing a line of circuit precedent holding that, when all patent claims were dismissed without prejudice, the Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction.
The court nevertheless heard EOFlow’s appeal on the merits and reversed the trade secret verdict in Insulet’s favor.
In deciding it had jurisdiction, the Federal Circuit’s reasoning went like this:
That sort of multistep analysis resting on conjecture about what might happen in a yet-to-be-filed case is, under both binding Supreme Court precedent and sound principles of judicial administration, the wrong way to decide jurisdiction.
As I argue in an amicus brief supporting Insulet’s pending petition for rehearing en banc, the correct question is, simply: what claims appear in the operative, well-pleaded complaint? In Insulet, the amended complaint contains no patent claims. So, the Federal Circuit does not have jurisdiction. End of story.
Instead, however, the Federal Circuit panel imagined a new patent infringement complaint that Insulet might file in the future, identified a defense EOFlow might raise, and hypothesized how a court would resolve that defense to conclude that the case currently before it did, in fact, arise under patent law.
The 1L civil procedure chestnut, Louisville & Nashville Railroad v. Mottley, fully resolves the jurisdictional dispute in the Insulet case. Under Mottley‘s “well-pleaded complaint rule,” arising under jurisdiction depends on the claims in the plaintiff’s complaint, not on defenses and not on issues that might arise later.
If there were any doubt, the Supreme Court reiterated just last year, in Royal Canin U.S.A., Inc. v. Wullschleger, that, under the well-pleaded complaint rule, an amendment eliminating claims (such as Insulet’s amendment to remove its patent claims) can “wipe the jurisdictional slate clean.”
Insulet isn’t the first time the Federal Circuit has relied on a hypothetical patent dispute to expand its jurisdiction. For instance, the circuit had long held that it had exclusive jurisdiction over state law malpractice cases against patent lawyers because the cases raised questions about what would have happened in a prior patent case had the lawyer not erred.
In Gunn v. Minton, the Supreme Court rejected that line of Federal Circuit precedent. Indeed, the Federal Circuit has a poor record before the Supreme Court on these sorts of jurisdictional or procedural questions.
In a recent study, Mark Lemley and I reviewed every patent-related case the Supreme Court has decided since the Federal Circuit began operating four decades ago. We found that the conventional wisdom about the Federal Circuit (that the Supreme Court is constantly correcting it on matters of substantive patent law) is overstated. Instead, where the Federal Circuit performs poorly is in patent-related cases raising questions of jurisdiction or procedure. In those cases (sixteen in total), the Supreme Court disagreed with the Federal Circuit fifteen times. Including in Gunn.
Those numbers reflect a recurring problem with the Federal Circuit. Congress created the court to provide uniformity and expertise in patent law, but the court has relied on those goals to expand its own authority (vis-à-vis state courts, district courts, and the regional circuits) while ignoring transsubstantive principles of federal law.
Insulet is another example. Instead of applying the well-pleaded complaint rule and sending that trade secret case to the First Circuit, the panel imagined a hypothetical future patent dispute (that might never actually arise) to keep the case in the Federal Circuit.
The en banc court should correct the panel’s error. As Ryan Vacca has shown, though, the Federal Circuit has used en banc review far less often in recent years than it did earlier in its history.
That development removes one of the few ways to correct mistakes of patent law without Supreme Court intervention. When a regional circuit errs, another circuit can disagree, prompting reconsideration or Supreme Court review. On patent law, the Federal Circuit speaks for the whole country.
Supreme Court review supplies a check, but the Court is hearing fewer patent cases than it did a decade ago.
Insulet gives the Federal Circuit a straightforward opportunity to correct itself, for the correct rule is simple: the court should (like all other federal courts) decide jurisdiction by looking at the operative complaint alone.
Paul R. Gugliuzza is the Thomas W. Gregory Professor of Law at University of Texas at Austin School of Law.

articles.title: 24 Days Late, Not Six Months: The Missing Judgment in Heidary v. Amazon
articles.content:
联邦巡回法院近日驳回了海达里（Massoud Heidary）对亚马逊公司的自行上诉案（Heidary v. Amazon.com Inc.，案号2026-2128，2026年9月21日判决，非判例性，全体法官参与）。根据28 U.S.C. § 2107(a)规定，上诉通知必须在判决后30天内提交，该期限为“强制性和管辖性”，无例外情形（Bowles v. Russell，551 U.S. 205，2007年）。此判决与今年早些时候的Brown v. United States案件判决模式一致。

马里兰地区法院法官Hurson于2026年1月8日驳回了海达里的专利侵权诉讼，但海达里的上诉通知直到7月31日才送达。上诉期限计算容易引发混淆，尤其是对于自行上诉的原告而言。联邦巡回法院的驳回令虽然结果可能正确，但分析过程遗漏了一步：判决书并未说明判决生效日期或30天期限的具体计算方式，仅提到上诉通知“超出了最后期限”。

问题在于计算严格期限时的混淆。有时期限是从驳回之日起算30天，有时则是180天，且延期申请必须由地区法院（而非上诉法院）处理，但延期条件极为严格。
articles.summary:
by Dennis Crouch

The Federal Circuit recently dismissed the pro se appeal in Heidary v. Amazon.com Inc., No. 2026-2128 (Fed. Cir. Sept. 21, 2026) (nonprecedential, per curiam).

Judge Hurson (D. Md.) dismissed Massoud Heidary's patent infringement complaint on January 8, 2026, and Heidary's notice of appeal did not arrive until July 31. The Federal Circuit's dismissal order was simple: the 30-day deadline of 28 U.S.C. § 2107(a) for filing a notice of appeal is "mandatory and jurisdictional" with no equitable exceptions. Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007). The order follows the same pattern as Brown v. United States from earlier this year. Dennis Crouch, Day 61, Patently-O (March 23, 2026).

Notice of appeal timing is a trap for the unwary, and here a pro se plaintiff was caught.  But, I think the court skipped a step in its analysis, even though the result is probably right.  The appellate order never says when the judgment was entered or when the 30 days ran out, only that the notice "was received outside the deadline."

The trap is set by confusion over calculating a hard deadline. In particular, sometimes the deadline is 30 days from the dismissal, and other times it is 180 days, and some relief can be granted for delay, but that deadline is very tight and can only be offered by the district court, not the appellate court.

articles.title: The Missing Inventor Problem
articles.content:
Fortress Iron公司向最高法院提出请求，要求重新审查联邦巡回法院无效其两项电缆护栏专利的决定，原因是缺少一位无法找到的联名发明人。Fortress Iron, LP诉Digger Specialties, Inc.案（2026年9月3日提交请求）。该案由Lourie法官代表全体大法官撰写判决书（171 F.4th 1310，联邦巡回法院，2026年），全院于6月驳回了复审申请。我曾撰文分析该判决，并随后发表了第二篇文章，询问在AIA废除第102(f)条后，无效规则的来源是什么。本文重点关注最高法院的审查请求，并引用了最高法院1868年在Agawam诉Jordan案中的发明人资格决定。

该发明是一种垂直电缆栏杆屏障，一种用于甲板、阳台或楼梯的护栏，其填充物为一组拉紧的垂直电缆。Fortress公司所有者提出了这一想法，一名员工绘制了设计图，并添加了一些详细特征。但在中国制造的原型出现了问题：电缆在拉紧时会旋转。华平黄（Hua-Ping Huang）建议使用方形开口和方形锥形配件来阻止旋转，同事世德林（Shih-Te Lin）则提出改进方案以增强护栏的强度。这些想法都被采纳，但专利上仅署名了Fortress的两名员工。在诉讼过程中，各方发现应将黄和林列为联名发明人。林被找到并由美国专利商标局（USPTO）添加，但找到黄的过程中遇到了困难。

这里的基本情况是，各方均同意华平黄对发明做出了贡献，应列为专利发明人。Fortress公司希望添加他，但黄在2016年离开了承包商，没有留下联系方式，Fortress无法找到他。Fortress公司辩称，无论如何，它仍拥有专利权，因为黄的贡献是“服务性发明创造”，即时归承包商所有，而承包商已将权利让渡给Fortress。USPTO的记录中没有黄的让渡记录。记录显示，权利从全洲亚德克斯（Quan Zhou Yoddex）转移到Fortress Iron，即使找到黄后，Fortress也只是取得了他同意被列为发明人的授权，而不是让渡。

在诉讼过程中，Fortress公司承认黄和林是联名发明人，并转向35 U.S.C. §256来修正专利。该条款提供了两种方式。根据第（a）款，USPTO主任可在所有相关方和受让人的申请下发放修正证书。Fortress公司为林使用了这一途径，但承认对黄不可用，因为无法找到他签字。

第256(b)款是法庭途径。它规定，通过法庭通知和听证所有相关方的方式，可以修正遗漏发明人的错误。Fortress公司辩称，黄并非相关方，因为他不持有任何所有权，缺乏提出自身第256款主张的资格，且只能从被列为发明人中受益。地方法院不同意这一观点，联邦巡回法院也维持了原判。

Lourie法官在判决书中写道，即使发明人已经让渡其权利，他们仍是专利体系的核心，联名发明人无论是否拥有任何权益，都是相关方。将该短语限制为其经济利益可能受损的群体会重写法律条文，且无论如何，没有人知道黄是否会从被列为发明人中受益。通知和听证是“补救的必要条件，而非仅仅是形式”。由于Fortress公司无法给予通知，错误无法纠正，法院最终得出结论，无法纠正的发明人资格错误会使专利无效。

黄现在已经被找到。他于2026年4月10日签署了《发明人声明》（37 C.F.R. §1.324(b)(1)），即联邦巡回法院判决后的第八天，Fortress公司于4月16日提交了文件。7月20日，一名监督专利审查员批准了请求，并将文件送至修正证书部门。此后尚未出具任何文件。但修正证书并不能撤销无效的判决。地方法院已经裁定这两项专利无效，联邦巡回法院也维持了原判。除非最高法院介入或Fortress公司根据第60(b)条获得判决救济，否则修正后的专利似乎对DSI公司仍然不可执行。其他被控侵权者也可以援引Blonder-Tongue Laboratories, Inc.诉University of Illinois Foundation案（402 U.S. 313，1971年）中的非互相问题预先阻却原则，对被宣告无效的专利提出抗辩。

（总字数约1500字）
articles.summary:
by Dennis Crouch

Fortress Iron has asked the Supreme Court to review the Federal Circuit's decision invalidating two of its cable-railing patents because an omitted coinventor could not be found. Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc., No. 26-362 (petition filed Sept. 3, 2026). Judge Lourie wrote the opinion below for a unanimous panel, 171 F.4th 1310 (Fed. Cir. 2026), and the full court denied rehearing in June. I previously wrote about the holding, and then followed up with a second post asking where the invalidity rule comes from now that the AIA has repealed Section 102(f). This post centers on the cert petition, and I also pull in the Supreme Court's 1868 inventorship decision in Agawam v. Jordan.

The invention is a vertical cable rail barrier, a railing whose infill is a set of tensioned vertical cables, of the kind used on a deck, balcony, or stairway. Fortress's owner had the idea and an employee sketched the design, adding some detailed features. But prototypes built in China had a problem: the cables rotated as they were being tensioned. Hua-Ping Huang suggested square openings and square swage fittings to stop the rotation, and a coworker, Shih-Te Lin, suggested changes to strengthen the rail. Both ideas went into the final product, but the patents named only the two Fortress employees. During litigation, the parties discovered that Huang and Lin should be added as inventors. Lin was located and added by the USPTO. But there was difficulty finding Huang.

So the basic setup here is that everyone agrees that Hua-Ping Huang contributed to the invention and should be named on the patents. Fortress wanted to add him. But Huang left the contractor in 2016 without leaving contact information, and Fortress could not locate him. Fortress argued that it owned rights regardless because the contribution was a "service invention-creation" immediately owned by the contractor who assigned rights to Fortress. No assignment from Huang appears in the USPTO records. The recorded chain runs from Quan Zhou Yoddex to Fortress Iron, and even after finding him Fortress took his consent to be named, not an assignment.

In the litigation, Fortress conceded that Huang and Lin were coinventors and turned to 35 U.S.C. § 256 to fix the patents. The statute offers two routes. Under subsection (a), the USPTO Director may issue a certificate of correction "on application of all the parties and assignees." Fortress used that route for Lin, but admitted it was unavailable for Huang, who could not be found to sign.

Section 256(b) is the courtroom route. It provides that the error of omitting an inventor can be corrected by the court "on notice and hearing of all parties concerned." Fortress argued that Huang is not a party concerned because he holds no ownership interest, would lack standing to bring his own Section 256 claim, and could only benefit from being named. The district court disagreed, and the Federal Circuit affirmed.

Judge Lourie wrote that inventors remain central to the patent system even after they assign their rights, and that a coinventor is a party concerned whether or not he owns anything. Limiting the phrase to those whose economic interests might be harmed would rewrite the statute, and in any event nobody knows whether Huang would be helped or hurt by being named. Notice and a hearing are "a prerequisite to relief, not a mere formality." Because Fortress could not give notice, the error could not be corrected, and the court ultimately concluded that an inventorship error that cannot be corrected invalidates the patent.

Huang has now been found. He signed a Statement of Inventor under 37 C.F.R. § 1.324(b)(1) on April 10, 2026, eight days after the panel opinion issued, and Fortress filed the papers on April 16. On July 20 a supervisory patent examiner granted the petitions and sent the files to the Certificates of Correction Branch. Nothing has issued since. But a certificate of correction does not undo a judgment of invalidity. The district court has already held the two patents invalid and the Federal Circuit has affirmed. Unless the Supreme Court intervenes or Fortress wins relief from the judgment under Rule 60(b), the corrected patents seemingly remain unenforceable against DSI. Other accused infringers could also invoke the invalidity ruling under Blonder-Tongue Laboratories, Inc. v. University of Illinois Foundation, 402 U.S. 313 (1971) (non-mutual issue preclusion applies to invalidated patents).
